_readme: THE ACT REGISTRY (DRE-2825). One file, read by everything.
An ACT is something the pipeline does on its own and then announces: a
refusal, a recovery, a hold or a progress act. Until this file existed
every act announced itself in prose and every reader scraped that prose
independently — ten tag constants scattered through scripts/reconcile.py,
the console pattern-matching separate string markers, a sweep deciding
'was that the bot' from an emoji prefix. The vocabulary was remembered in
six places instead of declared in one.
THE FOURTH KIND (DRE-3389). `progress` is the ordinary life of a card,
and it was the hole the first three left. A refusal, a recovery and a
hold are all things that happen when something has gone wrong, so the
seven acts carrying a cadence were every one of them a recovery, and the
console's pulse had a bound to compare against only in the hour after a
fix attempt or a sweep. The CEO's recording of production on 2026-09-08
11:20 PT shows every row still. The three acts below — a build's
heartbeat, a review run, the gate's re-check — say the ordinary work is
still moving, and a healthy card now has a bound to pulse against.
A PROGRESS ACT HOLDS NOTHING AND REPAIRS NOTHING. It is never a hold and
never a recovery; it leaves the work `unchanged` and hands it to nobody
new. AND THE IDEMPOTENCY-KEY RULE BELOW DOES NOT APPLY TO IT — a
heartbeat repeats by design, five times a build, so its tag is not a
suppression key and nothing counts receipts that carry one. That is why
all three declare `adopted: false`: not 'a later card will emit it', but
'this tag is not, and will not become, a live key'. The check still
proves the tag is absent from the tree, which is what keeps the claim
honest.
Their cadences are MEASURED, not read off a job timeout — nothing times
a healthy build. DRE-3388 measured all three against live Actions runs on
2026-09-08 and declared them in the console's console/backend/receipts.py
FIRST; this file copies them, and scripts/check_act_consumers.py reads
both and fails on any difference. Each row's `why` carries the
measurement, so no round number stands here without one.
THE SIX RELEASE ACTS (DRE-3521) are the same kind, one per stage of a
release-train run: CI green, cut, build, roll out, verify, live. They
follow the three above in every respect — `adopted: false`, `state:
unchanged`, nothing discharged — and the numbers are the console's
again, declared in receipts.py by DRE-3518 and copied here. Nothing in
this tree emits any of them: the train relays the surface script's
output AFTER the script exits (scripts/release_train.py, run_surface),
so the run's log carries no stage timestamps, and each stage is
recorded by the caller's surface script as a GitHub deployment status
(agent-bureau DRE-3519) which the console reads. `release-live`
declares a null cadence: nothing follows a landed release, so the
console renders it complete rather than overdue. docs/pipeline-acts.md
carries the table.
Per act: the TAG it is keyed on, its KIND, the STATE it leaves the work
in, the NEXT ACTOR, what it DISCHARGES, its SUBSCRIBER — the workflow
expected to act on it — and its CADENCE, how often it is expected to
speak.
CADENCE (DRE-3298). `cadence_s` is the longest silence, in seconds, after
which this act's work should be read as stuck, and `cadence_why` is one
sentence saying where that number came from. Together with a recent act
they are the two inputs deriveLiveness (DRE-2852) turns into the One
River row's pulse and the sweep across the current stage of its journey
bar. The pipeline supplied neither, so every row on the live console read
`unknown` and stood still.
The rule is mechanical and every number is read off something that
already runs here. An act whose STATE is `dispatched` has a run coming
back, and its cadence is that run's own job timeout — 65 minutes for
qa-review.yml's review job, 120 for agent-fix.yml's fix job. Every other
act has handed the work to a person; no workflow declares how long a
person takes, so the cadence is `null` and the sentence says so.
`null` IS A DECLARATION, NOT AN OMISSION. The console renders it as
'parked' and never as 'overdue', so a row that leaves the field out fails
the check rather than being defaulted — a defaulted cadence is a number
nobody chose, rendered as a claim about a specific act. A cadence_s that
is neither a positive whole number nor null fails, and so does a
cadence_why that says nothing, for a null exactly as for a number: a
number nobody can explain is a guess wearing a data type.
The cadence is DATA THE PIPELINE DECLARES ABOUT ITSELF. It does not
belong in the frontend — the console's liveness.guard.test.ts fails any
component that types a cadence as a number — and it is not on the
trailer either: a reader takes it off this file, and putting it on a
receipt would move every receipt body this pipeline has ever posted,
which is exactly what the warning below forbids.
THE TRAILER IS ADDITIVE. THIS IS THE PART TO GET RIGHT.
The tags below are not prose. They are IDEMPOTENCY KEYS and PER-SHA
BUDGET COUNTERS: reconcile suppresses a repeat notice with `tag in body`,
and _worker_receipt_count enforces CRASHED_REVIEW_RETRY_CAP and
DEPENDABOT_RECEIPT_CAP by counting the receipts that carry one. Change the
grammar and every in-flight pull request's existing receipts become
invisible: budgets re-arm from zero and suppressed comments re-post. So
this file ADOPTS those tags as data — `adopted: true` — and
pipeline_act.receipt() reproduces the existing body BYTE-IDENTICALLY,
appending a trailer and nothing else. No constant is deleted, and
reconcile._AGENT_COMMENT_PREFIXES in particular stays until every
commenter emits a trailer; its removal is a separate, later card.
`adopted: false` means the act has a live receipt but no idempotency key
yet, so its tag is declared here and emitted by a later card. The check
proves such a tag is genuinely absent from the tree — the registry cannot
quietly claim an emission it does not have.
NAMES ARE NOT TAGS, and that is load-bearing. A trailer carries its own
act's name and the name of whatever it discharges; if a name contained
another act's tag, an idempotency check keyed on that tag would read this
receipt as the other act's and suppress it forever — the additive trailer
would stop being additive. problems() refuses it.
SUBSCRIBER IS DECLARED HERE AND RESOLVED ELSEWHERE. Asserting that every
subscriber names a workflow that exists and accepts that trigger is
DRE-2827, and it has to be an extension of the shipped
scripts/check_workflow_watchers.py: `workflow_call` reusables run under
the CALLER's workflow name, and most bureau-pipeline workflows are
reusables. A second, independent derivation of the same fact beside the
shipped one is the hazard this epic exists for.
JSON, not YAML: scripts/reconcile.py imports the reader on every product
repo's sweep, where there is no pip install and PyYAML is not guaranteed.
THE `unconverted` BLOCK (DRE-2826). Emission is enforced by
scripts/check_act_receipts.py: every `gh pr comment`, `gh issue comment`,
`_post_pr_note` and `linear_ops.cmd_comment` call in scripts/ and
.github/workflows/ either composes its body through pipeline_act.receipt()
or is named below, with the reason it does not. Nothing else passes, so a
recovery added in a hurry fails CI instead of posting a receipt nothing
downstream can read.
The fourth call form is the one that matters most and the one the card's
own corpus missed: a CARD comment never touches `gh`, it goes straight to
the Linear GraphQL API, and eight of the ten reconcile.py sites this epic
converts post that way. Reading only the `gh` forms would leave the guard
false on the day it merged, exactly where the traffic is.
The block is the record of the debt, not a mute button. A row must match
EXACTLY ONE receipt site (a row matching none has outlived the site it
excused; one matching two is excusing a site nobody chose), must carry a
reason, and must disappear the moment that site starts composing. Three
kinds: `not-an-act` — a verdict, a record or a report, which creates no
obligation and hands the work to nobody, so a trailer would answer
questions it was never asked; `undeclared-act` — act-shaped, with no row
in `acts` above; `seam` — a helper that posts a body its CALLERS own, the
shape `_post_pr_note` has, so converting it means converting the callers
and teaching the guard a second exclusion. Every `undeclared-act` row is a
candidate for the registry, and giving it one is a registry change rather
than an emission change.
Check this file against the code that emits it:
python3 scripts/pipeline_act.py check
What the act IS, in three words the whole pipeline can share. The kind
is not severity: a hold can be routine and a refusal can be trivial.
The first three are all things that happen when something has gone
wrong; `progress` (DRE-3389) is what a card does when nothing has.
kinds.refusal: The pipeline declined to act, and says why. The work stays exactly where it was.
kinds.recovery: The pipeline acted to move the work on by itself — a dispatch, a re-dispatch, a restart.
kinds.hold: The pipeline stopped and handed the work to a person. Nothing else is coming until they act.
kinds.progress: The ordinary work is still moving, and this is it saying so. It holds nothing and repairs nothing — the work is left exactly as it was, with the same actor still on it — and its tag is not an idempotency key, because a heartbeat repeats by design.

_readme: The state the act leaves the WORK in — the card or the pull request —
never the state of the run that took the act. A reader asks 'what is
true now', and these are the only four answers.
states.unchanged: Nothing moved. The notice is the whole act, and it is on the record.
states.held: Stopped and labelled for a person; no run will be dispatched at it.
states.escalated: Moved into a human queue lane — the work is now somebody's to answer.
states.dispatched: A run has been dispatched and is expected to report back.

acts.name: merge-ref-refreshed
acts.means: This pull request was red only on checks that were red on its merge base too and are green on `main` now, so the sweep merged `main` into the branch to get it a fresh merge ref.
acts.cadence_why: The refreshed head re-runs the review, whose bound is the review job timeout-minutes: 65 in .github/workflows/qa-review.yml.
acts.why: DRE-3144, from agent-bureau #2240 and #2241 (2026-09-02). Both went red on `Console backend (pytest)` because of a fault on `main` (DRE-2962); the fix merged at 00:02 and both stayed red until an operator ran `gh pr update-branch` by hand at 00:23 — #2240 with a critic APPROVE already sitting behind a failure that no longer existed. A RERUN CANNOT FIX IT: `gh run rerun` re-runs the same jobs against the SAME merge commit, and the merge ref was computed before the fix, so only a new head helps. AT MOST ONCE PER `main` COMMIT: the receipt opens with `stale-merge-ref-refresh @<main sha>` and that marker is the idempotency key, backed by a lifetime cap per pull request whose zero is the operator's fleet-wide off switch. THE VERDICT CARRIES: an update-branch-only head change leaves the three-dot diff unchanged, so content binding (DRE-2340) keeps the standing critic verdict and `should_review_pr.py` skips the re-review — the receipt says so, and says when it will not carry. The next actor is the review stub because the refreshed head is what re-runs CI and, when the diff did change, the critic.

acts.why: Past the retry cap the stall is reported rather than retried — a bounded vendor-boundary retry, the DRE-1921 lesson. It discharges the re-dispatch: the obligation that act created was 'a verdict will post', and this is the other way that obligation ends.

acts.name: conflict-agent-dispatched
acts.means: A pull request went DIRTY, so the conflict sweep dispatched the fix agent in conflict mode to merge the default branch into it.
acts.cadence_why: The dispatched conflict-resolution run's own bound: .github/workflows/agent-fix.yml gives its fix job timeout-minutes: 120.
acts.why: A conflicted pull request emits no workflow events at all — GitHub cannot build a merge commit, so no CI runs and the merge gate's DIRTY path never fires (PR #25 sat 17 minutes for a hand-nudge). The receipt is the dispatch announcement the fix run posts; it carries no idempotency key today, because the busy-guard rather than a marker is what bounds it.

acts.means: The conflict sweep could not run, so no fix agent was dispatched for this conflicted pull request.
acts.cadence_why: Null: the sweep dispatched nothing, so nothing is expected to report — .github/workflows/linear-sync.yml declares no bound, and its own comment measures the cron backstop arriving 78-100 minutes apart rather than every 15.
acts.why: DRE-3042. The act above is what SHOULD happen to a DIRTY pull request; this one is what the pipeline says when it cannot. The dispatcher used to fail into silence: linear-sync's conflict sweep exited 1 on 2026-09-03 and PR #244 sat DIRTY with no critic, no fix loop and no notice for twelve minutes, because a conflicted pull request emits no workflow events for anything else to hang a signal on. The 15-minute cron sweep is the automatic backstop, so the state the PR is left in is unchanged rather than held — but nobody is told by the backstop, and the operator is who acts if it does not arrive.

acts.name: fix-attempt-landed
acts.means: The fix agent pushed a new commit, so CI and the critic review re-run on it.
acts.cadence_why: The re-triggered review's own bound: .github/workflows/qa-review.yml gives its review job timeout-minutes: 65.
acts.why: Only a NEW commit re-triggers CI and the critic; the workflow verifies the head sha actually advanced before saying this, because announcing 'review re-running' when it did not is a lie that stalls the card in the review lane (DeltaSolv PR #74).

acts.name: fix-attempt-disputed
acts.means: The fix agent hit a blocker — it disagrees with the reviewer's blocking finding and stopped rather than force a change it believes is wrong.
acts.cadence_why: Null: the fixer pushed nothing and the card is parked for a human, and .github/workflows/agent-fix.yml declares no bound on that decision.
acts.why: The fixer pushed nothing, so the branch holds a stale REQUEST_CHANGES the critic will never lift on its own. The card is parked for a human rather than left to stall invisibly in the review lane. Its answer is picked up by the sweep and discharged by `fix-loop-restarted`.

acts.name: fix-finding-refuted
acts.means: The fix agent answered the reviewer's blocking finding with evidence the reviewer could not read and pushed nothing, so the pipeline re-dispatched ONE review of the same commit with that evidence attached.
acts.cadence_why: The one re-dispatched review's own bound: .github/workflows/qa-review.yml gives its review job timeout-minutes: 65.
acts.why: The sibling of `fix-attempt-disputed`, and the difference is who is being asked. A blocker asks a HUMAN because the fixer cannot settle the disagreement; a refutation settles it with evidence and needs only the reviewer to look again — the two agents are built to see different things (the critic holds no Linear key on purpose, DRE-2696), so a finding the fixer disproves is evidence the critic never had. The tag is ADOPTED because it is the per-head idempotency key in the same receipt: `refuted-finding @<sha8>` is what the fix loop counts to allow exactly ONE re-review per commit, and what qa-review.yml reads back to put the refutation in the critic's context. A second refutation on the same head is a loop, not a re-review, and escalates as `fix-attempt-disputed` does.

acts.name: run-failure-diagnosed
acts.means: A workflow failed twice — the original run and one automatic retry — so the medic diagnosed it in plain English on the card.
acts.cadence_why: Null: the retry already happened and the diagnosis is written for a person to read, so .github/workflows/medic.yml declares no bound on what they do next.
acts.why: Not a transient flake by the time it gets here: the retry already happened, and on a critic infra-crash or an upstream 5xx the medic deliberately neither retries nor diagnoses, because re-running against an exhausted limit cannot succeed and only deepens it (DRE-1921). The body is written by the diagnosis agent, so the anchor pins the WRITE CALL rather than any wording.

emits.note: The medic's report is agent-authored prose, so there is no fixed wording to pin. The anchor is the write call in the medic's own prompt — the point at which the receipt is emitted.

acts.name: retry-declined
acts.means: The medic declined its one automatic retry of a failed run — the card is parked for a human, or the run died of turn exhaustion, which a rerun cannot fix.
acts.cadence_why: Null: the one automatic retry is declined and nothing is started, so scripts/medic_retry.py leaves the card exactly where whoever parked it put it.
acts.why: DRE-2954. On 2026-09-01 the turn cap parked DRE-2937 in Backlog with needs-human at 16:36 and the medic re-ran its first dead run at 16:37 — a third ~$16 build on a card the pipeline itself had just called unbuildable, killed by hand twelve minutes later. Two mechanisms, each right alone, with nothing joining them. A refusal rather than a hold: the medic changes nothing about the card, it only declines to start a run at it, and whoever parked the card is still the next actor. The receipt exists so the next operator reading the run sees a DECISION rather than a miss — silence here reads identically to the gate never having been asked.

acts.name: proof-observation-pending
acts.means: A proof card is waiting on an observation nobody can make yet — the thing it exists to watch has not happened — so it names what is still to be observed and what would let it be observed.
acts.cadence_why: Null: the hold waits on an observation only a person can make, and scripts/linear_ops.py declares no bound on when they are able to make it.
acts.why: DRE-3275. A proof answers 'did it work', observed against real state (standards/card-quality.md), and some proofs cannot start: DRE-3135 needed a failing agent pull request in a console repo to EXIST before anyone could watch the pipeline handle it. That hold was typed by hand on 2026-09-06 as ordinary prose, so nothing read it — the card looked silent, and a silent card is what every backstop here is built to notice. With the row, `linear_ops.py proof-waiting` composes the line through the one receipt writer and the console's receipts.py renders `Waiting for proof — <reason>`. It discharges NOTHING: a hold is the start of an obligation, not the end of one. What ends it is `🔬 proof-observed: <what was observed>` — a plain comment, deliberately NOT a row of its own, the way a critic verdict ends a re-dispatch without being an act. Giving the discharge a row would put this act's live key on the comment that discharges it, and the next reader would find a fresh hold where the observation is; it is declared in `unconverted` as the record it is. The subscriber is the sweep, which is what reads a hold on a card and leaves it alone; the reader that renders it is the console, and resolving subscribers against real workflows is DRE-2827. The two halves are refused when they carry `budget exhausted` or `holding for a human`, because the console's enrich.HOLD_MARKERS reads either phrase as a fix-budget hold and would render this card as the wrong kind of stuck.

acts.name: build-heartbeat
acts.means: The build agent posted its ⏳ n/5 phase comment — the ordinary sign that a card being built is still moving.
acts.cadence_why: Measured, not read off a job timeout — nothing times a healthy build. 6300 s is DRE-3388's longest observed green heartbeat gap (69.7 min across 245 gaps, 2026-09-08) plus a 50% margin; it is declared in the console's console/backend/receipts.py and this file is held equal to it by scripts/check_act_consumers.py.
acts.why: The build's PROGRESS act, and the reason this kind exists. Every act carrying a cadence before it was a `recovery`, so the console could compare a row against a bound only in the hour after a fix attempt or a sweep, and the CEO's recording of production on 2026-09-08 11:20 PT shows every row still. MEASURED (DRE-3388, 2026-09-08 15:10 PT, against live Actions runs on agent-bureau and bureau-pipeline): the last 50 completed agent-task runs per repo — 100 runs, of which 74 finished green and all 74 matched a card — giving 245 consecutive ⏳ n/5 gaps. Longest gap on a green run 69.7 min (4181 s), DRE-3165 run 34045232203 on 2026-09-06, `1/5 plan formed` 09:25 PT to `3/5 green` 10:35 PT on a 93-minute devops build; the next three were 60.1 min (DRE-3115), 38.6 min (DRE-3251) and 35.8 min (DRE-3113). Plus a 50% margin: 6272 s, rounded up to 6300 s. It holds nothing and repairs nothing, so it is never a hold and never a recovery, and the idempotency-key rule does not apply to it — a heartbeat repeats by design, five times a build. Nothing new is posted for it: the receipt already exists, and this row is what lets a reader compare its age against a bound.

acts.name: review-run
acts.means: The adversarial critic is running on this head — the ordinary sign that a card in review is still moving.
acts.cadence_why: Measured, not read off the review job's timeout: 3000 s is DRE-3388's longest observed GREEN review duration (32.7 min, 2026-09-08) plus a 50% margin, which is shorter than the 65-minute wall a crashed run waits out. It is declared in the console's console/backend/receipts.py and this file is held equal to it by scripts/check_act_consumers.py.
acts.why: A card in review is doing ordinary work, not being repaired, and until this row nothing said how long that may go quiet. MEASURED (DRE-3388, 2026-09-08 15:10 PT, against live Actions runs on agent-bureau and bureau-pipeline): the last 50 completed qa-review runs per repo — 100 runs, 90 of them green. Longest green duration 32.7 min (1960 s), agent-bureau run 34187198542, 2026-09-07 21:30 PT to 22:02 PT; the next two were 23.4 min and 19.1 min. Plus a 50% margin: 2940 s, rounded up to 3000 s. Deliberately NOT the review job's `timeout-minutes: 65`: that is how long a review may hang before the runner kills it, and this is how long a review that is working takes. The recovery acts that wait on a crashed review keep the 3900 s bound; a healthy one is expected to speak sooner. Nothing new is posted for it — the console reads the run from GitHub.
